rv.q: It is the most politically pertinent play of the decade.
You are unlikely to see anything in the West End that comes with the same amounts of tension, combative intellectual complexity and sheer bare-toothed drama as Icke's reworking.
Icke's drama plays out like a thriller, balancing principle against pragmatism and faith against reason, spinning a cat's cradle of personal ambitions and agendas.

He has borrowed the framework from Arthur Schnitzler’s 1912. Vienna-set play in which a Jewish doctor refuses to let a Catholic priest minister to a patient, and expanded and updated it to here and now. To brilliant and blistering effect, detonating the hot topic of identity politics.
No play in the past 10 years has felt more tense, challenging, and intellectually provoking than this one.
Icke's rigorous, visceral rethink...is a vital and immensely timely addition to the West End.
At almost three hours, it's a long evening, yet it's a hugely rewarding one too.
The evening manages to be compelling and irritatingly voguish at the same time.
Impeccably executed stagecraft, inspired writing, and a terrific central performance fuse into a remarkable and revelatory piece of theatre.
Juliet Stevenson's unquenchable, indefatigable performance is transcendent. It has to be seen to be believed.
This is a production that holds the attention drawing fine performances from the whole cast with Juliet Stevenson its vibrant centre.
The Doctor is the dramatic equivalent of a scientific breakthrough.
It's a sharp-tongued vivisection of identity politics, anchored by an astonishing lead performance from Juliet Stevenson.
Deep, thoughtful and intense, there's sometimes so much shouting going on that one wonders if this is a play or a soap opera.
What a mirthless, artless farrago of jabber this is.

So yes, it's worth the ticket... yet although it is mesmeric, probably one to see if you want three hours of serious theatre, there is something about the play's translation to a big traditional theatre that doesn't quite gell.

cn.t: Critics praise this rigorous, vital drama as a rewarding exploration of complex moral questions, though at nearly three hours it demands patience from audiences.
